items.stem: Identify the term for the following: “A model in which rational consumers choose the option with the highest expected value or satisfaction”.
items.answer: Utility theory
items.markingKey: Utility theory: a model in which rational consumers choose the option with the highest expected value or satisfaction. [1]

items.stem: Assertion (A): Consumers do not always behave as utility theory predicts. Reason (R): People have limited time, information and cognitive capacity (bounded rationality). Choose the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
items.answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
items.markingKey: Bounded rationality leads to satisficing. [1]

items.stem: Explain the difference between utility theory and satisficing.
items.answer: Utility theory assumes consumers evaluate all options and choose the one with the greatest expected utility (maximising); satisficing assumes they stop searching once they find an option that is good enough, because time and information are limited.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each, contrasted [2]

items.stem: Freya is offered a choice in a promotion at a store in Dubai: Option A — a guaranteed voucher worth $30. Option B — a 50% chance of winning $200 (otherwise nothing). Calculate the expected value of Option B.
items.markingKey: 50% × $200 = 0.5 × 200 = $100. 1 mark method; 1 mark answer [2]

items.stem: Yusuf is offered a choice in a promotion at a store in Doha: Option A — a guaranteed voucher worth $150. Option B — a 10% chance of winning $400 (otherwise nothing). (a) Calculate the expected value of Option B. (b) Use prospect theory to explain why many people would choose Option A even if Option B had a higher expected value.
items.answer: (a) $40 (b) For gains, people are risk-averse: a certain gain is preferred to a gamble, because the possible disappointment of getting nothing weighs heavily.
items.markingKey: (a) 10% × $400 = 0.1 × 400 = $40. 1 mark method; 1 mark answer [2] (b) 1 mark risk-averse for gains; 1 mark explained [2]

items.stem: Mei is offered a choice in a promotion at a store in Hanoi: Option A — a guaranteed voucher worth $170. Option B — a 50% chance of winning $200 (otherwise nothing). (a) Calculate the expected value of Option B. (b) Explain how the choice could be reframed as a loss and how this might change behaviour.
items.answer: (a) $100 (b) If customers were first given $200 and told they would lose $30 for certain or face a 50% chance of losing it all, prospect theory predicts more would gamble, because people are risk-seeking for losses.
items.markingKey: (a) 50% × $200 = 0.5 × 200 = $100. 1 mark method; 1 mark answer [2] (b) 1 mark loss frame; 1 mark risk-seeking prediction [2]

items.stem: “Prospect theory as an explanation of consumer decision-making has more strengths than weaknesses.” Evaluate this view, including individual differences in your answer.
items.answer: Strength (usefulness): Retailers use framing (for example “avoid losing your discount”) to influence choices. Strength (supporting evidence): Experiments show consistent loss aversion and framing effects across many samples. Weakness (ecological validity): Much evidence comes from hypothetical gambles in questionnaires rather than real purchases. Weakness (individual differences): People differ in risk attitudes and loss aversion, which the model does not fully explain. Conclusion: a reasoned judgement about the overall value of the study.

items.stem: What is meant by ‘utility theory’?
items.answer: A model in which rational consumers choose the option with the highest expected value or satisfaction.
items.markingKey: Utility theory: a model in which rational consumers choose the option with the highest expected value or satisfaction. 1 mark for a partial definition; 2 marks for a full, accurate definition [2]

items.stem: A student writes: “Prospect theory assumes that people evaluate the final amount of wealth they will have.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. It assumes people evaluate gains and losses relative to a reference point.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: correct judgement; 1 mark: accurate explanation [2]

items.stem: Explain the main features of prospect theory.
items.answer: Outcomes are judged as gains or losses relative to a reference point; losses loom larger than gains (loss aversion); people are risk-averse for gains but risk-seeking for losses; small probabilities are overweighted.
items.markingKey: 1 mark reference point; 1 mark loss aversion; 1 mark risk attitudes [3]

items.stem: Elena is offered a choice in a promotion at a store in Cape Town: Option A — a guaranteed voucher worth $30. Option B — a 75% chance of winning $1000 (otherwise nothing). What is the expected value of Option B?

Write a non-directional (two-tailed) hypothesis for this study.
items.answer: There will be a difference in purchases per 100 visitors between shoppers shown 6 flavours and shoppers shown 24 flavours.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: IV and DV both included (operationalised); 1 mark: correct form of hypothesis [2]

items.stem: Discuss the extent to which consumers make rational decisions when they buy products. In your answer, you may refer to models of decision-making, cognitive biases and usefulness.
items.answer: Arguments for: Utility theory assumes consumers compare options and choose the one with the greatest expected value. For expensive purchases, many consumers search for information and compare features. Arguments against: Simon’s satisficing shows consumers often accept the first “good enough” option. Prospect theory shows losses loom larger than gains and choices change with framing. Heuristics, anchoring and choice overload (Iyengar and Lepper, 2000) lead to non-rational choices. Conclusion: a supported judgement weighing the evidence on both sides.

items.stem: Freya set up a tasting stand in a supermarket in Lima. On 10 days it showed 24 flavours of jam and on 10 days it showed 6 flavours. The number of jars bought (per 100 visitors to the stand) was recorded each day. Table: Jars bought per 100 visitors — 6 flavours: 19, 18, 15, 20, 12, 20, 21, 18, 20, 12. 24 flavours: 6, 2, 3, 0, 6, 7, 0, 6, 9, 4. (a) Identify the independent variable (IV) and the dependent variable (DV) in this study. (b) Calculate the mean score for each condition. Give your answers to one decimal place. (c) To what extent do these results support the prediction that shoppers shown 6 flavours will buy more jars per 100 visitors than shoppers shown 24 flavours? Use the data in your answer. (d) Suggest one improvement to this study and explain how it would improve the validity or reliability of the results.
items.answer: (a) IV: the number of flavours on display (6 or 24). DV: the number of jars bought per 100 visitors to the stand each day. (b) 6 flavours: 17.5; 24 flavours: 4.3. (c) Mean for 6 flavours = 17.5 and 24 flavours = 4.3; the direction of the difference matches the prediction and the scores in the two conditions do not overlap and the sample is small (n = 10 per condition), so the results support it, although the small sample limits confidence; a statistical test would be needed to show the difference is significant. (d) Use a larger sample with more participants in each condition, so that anomalous individuals have less effect and the results are more reliable and generalisable.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: IV; 1 mark: DV, operationalised [2] (b) 6 flavours: 175 ÷ 10 = 17.5; 24 flavours: 43 ÷ 10 = 4.3. 1 mark for each correct mean [2] (c) 1 mark: uses both means; 1 mark: judgement about direction; 1 mark: limitation such as overlap of scores, small sample or no statistical test [3] (d) 1 mark: improvement; 1 mark: how to do it; 1 mark: effect on validity/reliability explained [3]

items.stem: Evaluate Iyengar and Lepper’s (2000) study of choice overload in terms of two strengths and two weaknesses. At least one of your evaluation points must be about ecological validity.
items.answer: Strength (usefulness): Retailers can simplify displays or product ranges to increase sales. Strength (ecological validity): It took place in a real supermarket with real shoppers making real purchases. Weakness (reliability): Later replications have not always found choice overload, suggesting the effect depends on conditions. Weakness (controls): Displays alternated by hour, but the shoppers present at different times may have differed. Conclusion: a reasoned judgement about the overall value of the study.

items.stem: Explain the difference between compensatory and non-compensatory decision rules.
items.answer: Compensatory rules weigh all attributes so that a weakness can be offset by a strength; non-compensatory rules (such as elimination by aspects) reject an option that fails on one attribute regardless of its other strengths.

items.stem: Explain how anchoring can influence how much consumers are willing to pay.
items.answer: An initial number, such as a high “original” price, becomes a reference point; later judgements are adjusted insufficiently from it, so a discounted price seems like good value.
items.markingKey: 1 mark anchor/reference point; 1 mark insufficient adjustment [2]

items.stem: Explain the difference between System 1 and System 2 thinking in buying decisions.
items.answer: System 1 is fast and intuitive, used for habitual or impulse purchases; System 2 is slow and analytical, used for expensive or important purchases where options are compared.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each with example [2]

items.stem: An online shop in Mexico City shows a coffee machine as “Was $450 — now $299. Only 2 left! 15 people are viewing this item.” Suggest how Tomás could use System 2 thinking to make a better decision.
items.answer: Slow down, compare prices and features across shops, and decide on a budget before seeing the anchor.

items.stem: An online shop in Dubai shows a coffee machine as “Was $450 — now $299. Only 2 left! 15 people are viewing this item.” (a) Identify two cognitive biases the shop is using. (b) Explain how one of these biases might lead Nadia to buy the machine.
items.answer: (a) Anchoring (was $450) and scarcity (only 2 left), plus social proof (15 people viewing). (b) The $450 anchor makes $299 seem like a large saving, so Nadia judges it as good value without comparing other shops.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each [2] (b) 1 mark bias; 1 mark effect [2]

items.stem: Evaluate research on anchoring in consumer decisions, including a discussion of ethics.
items.answer: Strength (usefulness): Consumers can be taught to recognise anchors and make better decisions. Strength (reliability): Anchoring effects have been replicated many times with different products and samples. Weakness (ethics): Retailers can use anchors to mislead consumers about value. Weakness (ecological validity): Many studies use hypothetical questions rather than real purchases. Conclusion: a reasoned judgement about the overall value of the study.

items.markingKey: System 1 thinking: fast, automatic, intuitive thinking that requires little effort. 1 mark for a partial definition; 2 marks for a full, accurate definition [2]

items.stem: With reference to research on anchoring in consumer decisions, explain one strength relating to usefulness.
items.answer: Consumers can be taught to recognise anchors and make better decisions.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies a relevant strength linked to usefulness; 1 mark: explained using detail from the study [2]

items.stem: Explain one weakness of research on anchoring in consumer decisions in terms of ethics.
items.answer: Retailers can use anchors to mislead consumers about value.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies a relevant weakness linked to ethics; 1 mark: explained using detail from the study [2]

items.stem: An online shop in Dubai shows a coffee machine as “Was $450 — now $299. Only 2 left! 15 people are viewing this item.” Suggest how Ravi could use System 2 thinking to make a better decision.
items.answer: Slow down, compare prices and features across shops, and decide on a budget before seeing the anchor.
items.markingKey: 1 mark strategy; 1 mark explained [2]

items.stem: Sofia set up a tasting stand in a supermarket in Karachi. On 8 days it showed 24 flavours of jam and on 8 days it showed 6 flavours. The number of jars bought (per 100 visitors to the stand) was recorded each day. Table: Jars bought per 100 visitors — 6 flavours: 14, 26, 21, 19, 40, 21, 22, 17. 24 flavours: 10, 5, 6, 3, 5, 8, 1, 4. (a) Calculate the percentage of participants in the 6 flavours condition who scored 14 or more. Show your working. (b) The standard deviation for the 6 flavours condition was 7.91 and for the 24 flavours condition was 2.82. Explain what these values show.
items.answer: (a) 100% (b) The 6 flavours condition has the larger standard deviation, so its scores are more spread out around the mean; the other condition’s scores are more consistent.
items.markingKey: (a) 8 out of 8 participants scored 14 or more: 8 ÷ 8 × 100 = 100%. 1 mark working; 1 mark answer [2] (b) 1 mark: identifies the condition with the larger spread; 1 mark: explains that a larger SD means scores are more spread around the mean [2]

items.stem: Discuss the strengths and weaknesses of research on anchoring in consumer decisions. Include at least one point about ecological validity.
items.answer: Strength (usefulness): Consumers can be taught to recognise anchors and make better decisions. Strength (reliability): Anchoring effects have been replicated many times with different products and samples. Weakness (ecological validity): Many studies use hypothetical questions rather than real purchases. Weakness (ethics): Retailers can use anchors to mislead consumers about value. Conclusion: a reasoned judgement about the overall value of the study.
items.markingKey: Levels of response. Top band: strengths and weaknesses are accurate, well explained and clearly linked to the study, the named issue is discussed, the answer is well organised and reaches a conclusion. Middle band: points are mostly accurate but one side is less developed or links to the study are general. Lower band: points are identified but brief, generic or one-sided. Description of the procedure without evaluation receives little credit.

items.stem: Identify the term for the following: “Kahneman and Tversky’s model in which choices are judged as gains or losses from a reference point, and losses loom larger than gains”.
items.answer: Prospect theory
items.markingKey: Prospect theory: Kahneman and Tversky’s model in which choices are judged as gains or losses from a reference point, and losses loom larger than gains. [1]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain the main features of prospect theory. (b) In a revision session, a student says: “Satisficing can reduce the time and effort involved in decisions.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: (a) Outcomes are judged as gains or losses relative to a reference point; losses loom larger than gains (loss aversion); people are risk-averse for gains but risk-seeking for losses; small probabilities are overweighted. (b) Correct. The search stops once an acceptable option is found.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark reference point; 1 mark loss aversion; 1 mark risk attitudes [3] (b) 1 mark: correct judgement; 1 mark: accurate explanation [2]

items.stem: With reference to prospect theory as an explanation of consumer decision-making, explain one strength relating to usefulness.
items.answer: Retailers use framing (for example “avoid losing your discount”) to influence choices.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies a relevant strength linked to usefulness; 1 mark: explained using detail from the study [2]

items.stem: Ana set up a tasting stand in a supermarket in Kuala Lumpur. On 8 days it showed 24 flavours of jam and on 8 days it showed 6 flavours. The number of jars bought (per 100 visitors to the stand) was recorded each day. Table: Jars bought per 100 visitors — 6 flavours: 23, 22, 26, 20, 23, 19, 19, 20. 24 flavours: 6, 3, 5, 8, 8, 3, 1, 6. Write a directional (one-tailed) hypothesis for this study.
items.answer: Shoppers shown 6 flavours will buy more jars per 100 visitors than shoppers shown 24 flavours.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: IV and DV both included (operationalised); 1 mark: correct form of hypothesis [2]

items.stem: Omar is offered a choice in a promotion at a store in Lagos: Option A — a guaranteed voucher worth $150. Option B — a 10% chance of winning $1000 (otherwise nothing). Calculate the expected value of Option B.
items.markingKey: 10% × $1000 = 0.1 × 1000 = $100. 1 mark method; 1 mark answer [2]

items.stem: In a replication of Iyengar and Lepper in Bogotá, purchases per 100 visitors were recorded on days with a large (24) or small (6) display of jams. Table: Jars bought per 100 visitors — 6 flavours: 24, 25, 18, 15, 18, 21, 22, 16. 24 flavours: 5, 0, 12, 4, 1, 9, 6, 6. Write a non-directional (two-tailed) hypothesis for this study.
items.answer: There will be a difference in purchases per 100 visitors between shoppers shown 6 flavours and shoppers shown 24 flavours.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: IV and DV both included (operationalised); 1 mark: correct form of hypothesis [2]

items.stem: A researcher in Manila is interested in how consumers decide which smartphone to buy. Design a questionnaire to test this. Your plan must include: one example question, ethical issues and how the data will be analysed.
items.answer: Method: a questionnaire. Closed questions (for example rating scales from 1 to 5) for quantitative data and at least one open question for qualitative detail; pilot the questions; avoid leading questions. Variables: topic: decision strategies; measure: open and closed questions. Sample: for example an opportunity or volunteer sample of about 30 people from the target population in Manila, with reasons. Design/procedure: clear, replicable steps, with standardised instructions and random allocation or counterbalancing where relevant. Ethics: informed consent, right to withdraw, protection from harm, confidentiality and a full debrief. Data: quantitative scores summarised with means and a suitable graph; qualitative answers analysed into themes where collected.
items.markingKey: Levels of response. Top band: a detailed, accurate and replicable plan using the stated method; all required features are included and are appropriate to the aim; variables are operationalised; ethics are addressed. Middle band: a workable plan with most required features but some lack detail or are not justified. Lower band: a basic plan with few features or with errors in method.

items.stem: Design a laboratory experiment to investigate whether presenting a price as a discount or as a “saving” changes willingness to buy. Your plan must include: the experimental design, the type of data collected and the sampling technique.
items.answer: Method: a laboratory experiment. Manipulate the IV in a controlled room; standardised procedure and instructions; measure the DV objectively. Variables: IV: discount frame or saving frame; DV: rating of willingness to buy (1–10). Sample: for example an opportunity or volunteer sample of about 30 people from the target population in Riyadh, with reasons. Design/procedure: clear, replicable steps, with standardised instructions and random allocation or counterbalancing where relevant. Ethics: informed consent, right to withdraw, protection from harm, confidentiality and a full debrief. Data: quantitative scores summarised with means and a suitable graph; qualitative answers analysed into themes where collected.
items.markingKey: Levels of response. Top band: a detailed, accurate and replicable plan using the stated method; all required features are included and are appropriate to the aim; variables are operationalised; ethics are addressed. Middle band: a workable plan with most required features but some lack detail or are not justified. Lower band: a basic plan with few features or with errors in method.

items.stem: Identify the term for the following: “Choosing the option that is best on the single most important attribute”.
items.answer: Lexicographic heuristic
items.markingKey: Lexicographic heuristic: choosing the option that is best on the single most important attribute. [1]

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Describe the procedure and findings of Iyengar and Lepper’s (2000) jam study. (b) In a revision session, a student says: “Heuristics save time but can lead to errors.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: (a) In a supermarket, a tasting booth displayed either 24 or 6 flavours of jam on alternate hours. More shoppers stopped at the large display (60% versus 40%) but far more of those who stopped at the small display bought jam (30% versus 3%). (b) Correct. They simplify decisions at the cost of accuracy.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark procedure; 1 mark stopping; 1 mark buying [3] (b) 1 mark: correct judgement; 1 mark: accurate explanation [2]

items.stem: Outline one strength of Iyengar and Lepper’s (2000) study of choice overload that relates to ecological validity.
items.answer: It took place in a real supermarket with real shoppers making real purchases.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies a relevant strength linked to ecological validity; 1 mark: explained using detail from the study [2]

items.stem: In a replication of Iyengar and Lepper in Seoul, purchases per 100 visitors were recorded on days with a large (24) or small (6) display of jams. Table: Jars bought per 100 visitors — 6 flavours: 15, 16, 17, 12, 14, 12, 20, 14. 24 flavours: 9, 0, 0, 2, 3, 5, 0, 6. Using the mean scores, state one conclusion that can be drawn from these results.
items.answer: The 6 flavours condition had a higher mean (15.0) than the 24 flavours condition (3.1), suggesting that a smaller choice set leads to more purchases (choice overload).
items.markingKey: 1 mark: conclusion about the effect of the IV on the DV; 1 mark: supported with the means [2]

items.stem: Amara recorded purchases by shoppers who stopped at displays of different sizes. 24-flavour display: bought 3, did not buy 114; 12-flavour display: bought 19, did not buy 83; 6-flavour display: bought 29, did not buy 69. (a) Calculate the percentage of shoppers for 6-flavour display that were “bought”. Give your answer to one decimal place. (b) Identify which row has the highest proportion of “bought” shoppers. Show how you worked this out.
items.answer: (a) 29.6% (b) 6-flavour display (29.6%)
items.markingKey: (a) 29 ÷ (29 + 69) × 100 = 29 ÷ 98 × 100 = 29.6%. 1 mark working; 1 mark answer [2] (b) 1 mark: percentages (or proportions) calculated for each row; 1 mark: correct row identified [2]

items.stem: Discuss whether consumers make rational decisions when they buy products. In your answer, you may refer to usefulness and models of decision-making.
items.answer: Arguments for: Utility theory assumes consumers compare options and choose the one with the greatest expected value. For expensive purchases, many consumers search for information and compare features. Arguments against: Simon’s satisficing shows consumers often accept the first “good enough” option. Prospect theory shows losses loom larger than gains and choices change with framing. Heuristics, anchoring and choice overload (Iyengar and Lepper, 2000) lead to non-rational choices. Conclusion: a supported judgement weighing the evidence on both sides.
items.markingKey: Levels of response. Top band: accurate, detailed psychological knowledge (named studies/theories) used to build a two-sided argument; evaluation includes issues such as validity, reliability, generalisability, ethics or usefulness; a justified conclusion. Middle band: relevant knowledge with some evaluation, but one side or the conclusion is underdeveloped. Lower band: limited, mostly descriptive answer with little evaluation.

items.stem: An online shop in Doha shows a coffee machine as “Was $450 — now $299. Only 2 left! 15 people are viewing this item.” (a) Explain how one of these biases might lead Kwame to buy the machine. (b) Suggest how Kwame could use System 2 thinking to make a better decision.
items.answer: (a) The $450 anchor makes $299 seem like a large saving, so Kwame judges it as good value without comparing other shops. (b) Slow down, compare prices and features across shops, and decide on a budget before seeing the anchor.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark bias; 1 mark effect [2] (b) 1 mark strategy; 1 mark explained [2]

items.stem: An online shop in Karachi shows a coffee machine as “Was $450 — now $299. Only 2 left! 15 people are viewing this item.” (a) Identify two cognitive biases the shop is using. (b) Explain how one of these biases might lead Grace to buy the machine. (c) Suggest how Grace could use System 2 thinking to make a better decision.
items.answer: (a) Anchoring (was $450) and scarcity (only 2 left), plus social proof (15 people viewing). (b) The $450 anchor makes $299 seem like a large saving, so Grace judges it as good value without comparing other shops. (c) Slow down, compare prices and features across shops, and decide on a budget before seeing the anchor.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each [2] (b) 1 mark bias; 1 mark effect [2] (c) 1 mark strategy; 1 mark explained [2]
